# Ecosystem Field Guide: What Real S7 Packages Teach

Each package below was verified against its current documentation or source
(September 2026). The interest is not in their domains but in the *design
moves* they demonstrate — each is the clearest available exhibit for at least
one pattern from the preceding documents. The guide is organized into five
thematic clusters, with cross-cutting observations at the end.

---

## Cluster A — Values, state, and architecture

### ellmer — the hybrid architecture, and dispatch as a plugin system

[ellmer](https://ellmer.tidyverse.org/) (tidyverse; LLM chat from R) is the
reference example for mixing object systems by semantics rather than
ideology. The [`Chat`](https://ellmer.tidyverse.org/reference/Chat.html)
object is **R6**, and the documentation is explicit about why: a conversation
is mutable state with identity — you send messages to *it*, it accumulates
turns, it runs the tool-invocation loop — and value semantics would force
callers to reassign after every exchange. Branching a conversation requires
an explicit `$clone()`, exactly the ceremony value semantics would have made
free, and ellmer accepts that trade consciously.

Everything flowing *through* the Chat is **S7 values**:
[`Turn`](https://ellmer.tidyverse.org/reference/Turn.html) (with `UserTurn`,
`SystemTurn`, `AssistantTurn` subclasses — a sum type as a subclass family,
where the assistant variant carries extra fields like tokens, cost, and
finish reason), `Content` objects inside turns (text, images, tool requests,
tool results — another variant family),
[`Model`](https://ellmer.tidyverse.org/reference/Model.html) (a small
immutable configuration value), and `Provider`. Records of fact are values;
the ongoing process is a reference.

The `Provider` hierarchy doubles as the package's plugin system: the README
lists ten official and nine community providers, and supporting a new LLM
service means subclassing `Provider` and registering methods on the existing
generic vocabulary for request building and response parsing. The data axis
of the expression problem, held open on purpose — community providers extend
ellmer without touching its core.

### ragnar — honest base-type inheritance and the enriched table

[ragnar](https://ragnar.tidyverse.org/) (tidyverse; retrieval-augmented
generation) contributes two small, perfect exhibits.

[`MarkdownDocument`](https://ragnar.tidyverse.org/reference/MarkdownDocument.html)
is an S7 class inheriting from **character**: a document *is* a length-one
markdown string, with an `@origin` property riding along. The inheritance
passes the honesty test of
[05-composition-and-dispatch.qmd](05-composition-and-dispatch.qmd) — treating
the object as text is semantically sound, not merely convenient. Its
constructor is a boundary parser in miniature: it *normalizes* (collapses
lines, enforces UTF-8) so that, quoting the docs, "downstream code can rely
on a consistent format" — parse-don't-validate stated as user documentation.

`MarkdownDocumentChunks` inherits from **tibble**: chunk data is genuinely
tabular (start, end, context columns; users will filter and mutate it), so it
should *be* a data frame — but it carries the source document as a
`@document` property, keeping the provenance attached to the value rather
than in a parallel variable the user must not lose. An enriched table:
structural behavior from the base class, domain identity and payload from S7.

### tooey — the Elm architecture as a whole-program design

[tooey](https://github.com/devOpifex/tooey) (devOpifex) is a terminal UI
framework built on the **Model–View–Update** architecture (The Elm
Architecture): an application is three pure functions — `init(model)`
producing initial commands, `update(model, msg)` mapping a state and a
message to a new state plus commands, and `view(model, buf)` rendering state
into a screen buffer — while a runtime loop owns the terminal, the clock, and
input events, feeding them in as messages (`is_key`, `is_tick`) and executing
returned commands (`cmd_tick`, `cmd_quit`).

This is the functional core / imperative shell of
[02-values-and-state.qmd](02-values-and-state.qmd) in its most disciplined
published form: *all* state transitions are pure data-to-data functions,
*all* effects are values (commands) interpreted by the shell, and the
framework — not convention — enforces the boundary. Even in a domain as
imperative-seeming as a live terminal UI, mutation is confined to a runtime
the application author never touches. It is also a working answer to
"where do messages and events fit in a value-oriented design": as plain data
dispatched over, exactly like any other variant family.

## Cluster B — Documents, schemas, and serialization

### stacbuildr — the document-object-model pattern, complete

[stacbuildr](https://github.com/stevenpawley/stacbuildr) (STAC geospatial
catalogs) is the fullest single exhibit of
[06-documents-schemas-dsls.qmd](06-documents-schemas-dsls.qmd): STAC 1.1.0
Catalogs, Collections, and Items as an S7 class graph, serialized to STAC
JSON, **validated against the published JSON schemas** (rung 0 delegated to
the specification's own authority), with extensions (electro-optical, raster,
projection, and more) layered onto the core following the spec's own shared
`bands` model.

Two moves stand out beyond the basics. First, the boundary-constructor
family: `item_from_terra()`, `item_from_sf()`, `item_from_lidr()` lift
*native* geospatial objects — rasters, geometries, point clouds users already
hold — into document nodes, extracting extents, projections, and band
metadata at the boundary. Second, the **document as data**: a Collection
supports `length()`, `[[`, `as.data.frame()` (one row per item, properties as
columns, list-columns for structured values), and `sf::st_as_sf()` — the
object graph projects into the tabular and spatial idioms R users already
know, rather than forcing graph navigation. Its `write_stac()` also encodes
the STAC best-practices catalog layouts (self-contained, relative, absolute)
as an explicit enum that maps one-to-one onto PySTAC's `CatalogType` —
cross-ecosystem vocabulary alignment as API design.

### S7schema — schema as boundary contract, productized

[S7schema](https://cran.r-project.org/package=S7schema) (Novo Nordisk; CRAN)
is the schema-as-boundary-contract posture as a reusable framework: YAML
configuration files validated against JSON Schema definitions using AJV (via
V8), with the resulting configuration objects inheriting from **both S7
classes and base lists** — full conformance checking delegated to the schema
ecosystem's standard tooling, R-side typing layered on for downstream
extension through custom classes and methods. Notably it does *not* re-derive
the schema's rules as property validators — the two layers check different
things.

### rapid — an external specification as a strict domain object

[rapid](https://github.com/api2r/rapid) (api2r) converts OpenAPI descriptions
into R objects of a new S7 class that, in its own words, "enforces a strict,
opinionated schema." The design posture is instructive: rather than wrapping
the OpenAPI JSON loosely, it parses the specification into a validated
domain object intended as the substrate for downstream *code generation*
(the beekeeper and mockplumber packages). An API description is exactly the
kind of declarative document [06](06-documents-schemas-dsls.qmd) describes,
and rapid is the front-end that makes it lawful before generators consume
it — parse once at the boundary, generate from the certified object.

### sqlr and its dialects — schema as the middle term, round-trip as oracle

[nbenn/sqlr](https://github.com/nbenn/sqlr) has matured into one of the most
architecturally articulate S7 packages anywhere, and its README states its
thesis in one sentence: what R lacked was "a representation of a schema that
is neither a string nor a connection, which you can build, render, reflect
and compare." That middle term — the schema as a first-class *value* between
the DDL text and the live database — is the document-object-model argument
made for SQL.

Four design moves reward study. **Dialects are objects, not connections**:
rendering (`sqlr_render(schema, sqlite())`) needs no server, no driver, and
the core package renders nothing on its own — dialect packages
(`sqlr.postgres`, `sqlr.sqlite`) supply the spellings via multiple dispatch
(`render_sql(x, con)` dispatching on object and dialect at once). **There is
deliberately no generic fallback**: nothing renders "ANSI SQL," because no
engine implements it faithfully and "an untestable default would quietly
accumulate behaviour no database had ever accepted" — an unregistered
dialect is an error rather than a guess. **Reflection closes the loop**:
`sqlr_reflect(con)` reads a live database's catalog back into the same
representation `sqlr_render()` consumes, and the round trip
(`sqlr_equal(schema, sqlr_reflect(con))`) is, in the package's own words,
"the package's own test oracle." **Equality is structural and semantic**:
constraints and indexes are matched on *what they constrain*, not their
order or auto-generated names, so a hand-written schema compares equal to a
reflected one — and `sqlr_diff()` reports meaningful differences, the
explicit groundwork for a future migration generator. Rendering even
performs real compilation work: tables emit in dependency order and
cycle-closing foreign keys are lifted into trailing `ALTER TABLE`
statements.

### typedjson — round-trip fidelity as the entire product

[typedjson](https://github.com/nbenn/typedjson) (same author) makes the
round-trip *law* of [06](06-documents-schemas-dsls.qmd) into a package: it
"writes an R value as JSON a human can read, and reads it back unchanged."
Its README diagnoses the existing landscape precisely — `jsonlite` is
readable but lossy (doubles return as integers, all-`NA` vectors lose their
type, empty typed vectors collapse to `list()`), `serializeJSON` is faithful
but unreadable — and stakes out the missing quadrant: ordinary JSON for
ordinary values, with annotations *only for what JSON cannot express*
(integer versus double, typed missing values, non-finite doubles,
attributes, language objects, and S3/S4/S7 objects). That principle —
annotate the minimum needed to make the round trip an identity — is the
presence-policy and wire-universe discussion of
[03-types-and-meaning.qmd](03-types-and-meaning.qmd) turned into a
serialization format.

### structr — the contrast case: a compiled schema, not an object system

[structr](https://github.com/ixpantia/structr) (ixpantia) is deliberately
*not* S7 — it is Rust (`serde`, `simd_json`) behind an R schema DSL
(`s_map()`, `s_integer()`, `s_optional()`, `build_structure()`) — and it
earns its place here as the boundary of the boundary. structr compiles a
schema once and then parses *and* serializes against it, strictly: type
mismatches, missing fields, and unexpected nulls are errors. It is rungs 0–1
of the checking ladder as a standalone, high-performance tool, with no
domain objects at all — the output is plain R lists that are *known* to
conform. The lesson is about division of labor: when the need is pure wire
conformance at speed, a compiled schema validator beats an object system,
and an S7 domain layer is what you build *on top of* such a boundary when
invariants, identity, and dispatch are needed beyond the parse. Its "all
fields required unless `s_optional()`" default is also the right polarity
for presence policy — opt into looseness, never out of it.

## Cluster C — Errors, contracts, and introspection

### resultr — errors as values, the Result/Option sum type

[resultr](https://github.com/TransGirlCodes/resultr) implements Rust's
`Result`/`Option` vocabulary in S7, and its
[`Result.R`](https://github.com/TransGirlCodes/resultr/blob/main/R/Result.R)
is a compact tour of the sum-type playbook: an abstract `Result` parent
"used for the purposes of dispatch," `Success` and `Failure` subclasses each
carrying one property, and the full monadic combinator set as generics —
`unwrap()`, `unwrap_or_default()`, `unwrap_or_else()`, `and_then()`,
`inspect()`, `expect()` — with per-variant methods (the `Failure` method for
`and_then` simply returns itself, which *is* railway-oriented
short-circuiting).

Three details are worth stealing. First, the **boundary between conditions
and values** is a generic: `wrap_in_result()` has methods for `class_any`
(wrap in `Success`), `class_error` and `class_warning` (wrap in `Failure`),
and `Result` itself (pass through) — so R's condition system is converted
into value-level errors at exactly one point, inside `and_then()`'s
`rlang::try_fetch()`. Second, **write-once properties**: both `@value` and
`@error` use a setter that errors if the slot is already set — a poor
man's immutability enforcement, making the certificate tamper-evident.
Third, `expect()` dispatches on `list(Success, class_character)` — multiple
dispatch pressed into service for argument typing. The broader lesson feeds
[04-parse-dont-validate.qmd](04-parse-dont-validate.qmd): R has *two* error
channels, conditions (control flow) and values (data flow), and a design
should choose per boundary which one crosses it.

### s7contract — interfaces, traits, and executable laws

[s7contract](https://github.com/sounkou-bioinfo/s7contract) (CRAN) imports
the Go-interface/Rust-trait worldview onto S7 dispatch, and its README now
shows the full progression. **Structural interfaces** are named sets of
required generics, checked by method availability
(`implements(Circle, Shape)`), with `missing_requirements()` reporting
exactly which verb is absent — Go's implicit satisfaction, made queryable.
**Traits** require explicit `impl_trait()` registration and support default
methods and associated constants — Rust's explicit opt-in. **Progressive
runtime checks** let an interface requirement carry argument and return
specifications, enforced in contract-scoped evaluation (`with(Interface,
expr)`), so a method that returns the wrong type fails at the call with a
typed message. **Generative laws** combine named generators, shrinking, and
tinytest expectations (`expect_law()`), testing the behavioral half of the
contract that no dispatch table can see. Its stated limits are as instructive
as its features: all checks are runtime, and passing generated cases proves
nothing universally — honest about what a dynamic language can and cannot
recover of Rust's compile-time story.

### datarr (reflect) — the metaobject payoff of classes-as-values

[datarr](https://github.com/SanD94/datarr) (package name `reflect`) builds
runtime **reflection** for base R and S7: immutable descriptor objects for
properties, methods, and callables, with explicit capability predicates. Its
[`s7.R`](https://github.com/SanD94/datarr/blob/main/R/s7.R) shows what S7's
classes-as-first-class-values design makes possible in ordinary R code:
`reflect_properties()` walks `class@properties` and the constructor's
formals to report each property's declared type, default presence,
requiredness (a formal equal to the empty symbol), validator presence, and
whether it is *inherited* (tracing the declaring class up the parent chain);
`reflect_methods()` enumerates a generic's method table and can attach S7's
own `method_explain()` dispatch trace; `reflect_callable()` distinguishes
generics, methods, and closures with their signatures. The descriptors are
themselves S7 objects — reflection modeled in the system being reflected.

Two further touches: `reflect_validate()` wraps `S7::validate()` with a
chained, classed condition (the error-design discipline of
[04](04-parse-dont-validate.qmd) applied to the metalevel), and
`reflect_check_project()` audits a *package* against declared conventions
(export naming policy, dependency policy, lifecycle documentation) —
conventions turned into executable checks, which is the same move as
s7contract's laws applied to project structure instead of object behavior.

## Cluster D — Systems built on S7 at scale

### rtemis — constraints as data, one declaration to rule four artifacts

[rtemis](https://github.com/rtemis-org/rtemis) (machine learning framework,
150+ stars) rewrote its entire supervised/unsupervised backend from R6 and
S3 onto S7, and its
[`010_Props.R`](https://github.com/rtemis-org/rtemis/blob/main/R/010_Props.R)
is the most sophisticated property foundation yet published. The core idea:
every `prop_*` factory attaches a **`PropertySpec`** — a nested S7 object in
which the property's type, bounds, enum, default, nullability, and roughly
twenty further axes are stored *as data rather than closures*. Because the
constraints are data, one declaration mechanically produces four artifacts:
the R validator, the default, a JSON Schema (via `S7_to_JSONSchema()`), and
downstream a TUI configuration form. This is the "one canonical artifact,
many projections" principle executed at the level of individual properties,
and it is the reverse arrow of schema-driven development: the model
*generates* the schema.

The spec's axes are a checklist of presence-and-arity distinctions most
designs never separate: `container` (none / array / map / matrix / table /
struct / factor, each with a documented rationale — a factor serializes as
`{levels, codes}` because a label array would lose level order and empty
levels); `broadcast` (a scalar stands for the whole container) kept mutually
exclusive with `tunable` (an array alongside a value is a *search space*,
one nesting level above the value's own type — the comment warns "a reader
must never infer one from the other's shape"); `tune_on_null` versus
`default_on_null` (two different meanings of NULL, declared rather than
guessed); `constant` (class identity) versus fixed-but-settable;
`applies_when` (conditional applicability among sibling properties, encoded
as data and checked centrally); and `data_bound` — validity constraints tied
to *training-data dimensions* (`n_features`, `n_cases`, class names) that
cannot be checked at construction and are instead resolved in one pass
against the data before any training begins.

Around this foundation sit two more discipline exhibits. **Factory-time
validation**: a PropertySpec's validator checks that the declared default
conforms to its own spec, so a bad declaration "fails at factory time —
i.e. at package load — rather than at first instantiation." **Eager
configuration validation**: the user-facing `setup_*()` functions
(`setup_LightGBM()`, `setup_GridSearch()`) construct validated configuration
values *before* a run that may train thousands of models, so user error
surfaces in milliseconds, not hours. There is even an authorship-policy
annotation (`agent_writable`) deliberately excluded from published schemas
because *who may set a property* can change while *what the property is*
cannot — a crisp example of keeping volatile policy out of stable contracts.

### quickr — S7 as a compiler's intermediate representation

[quickr](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/quickr) (Tomasz Kalinowski; CRAN)
compiles R functions to Fortran. Users annotate functions with an
in-language type DSL — `declare(type(x = double(NA)))`, a runtime no-op the
compiler reads, expressing element modes, shapes, and *size relationships
between arguments* (`double(n)` twice means "same length") — and `quick()`
lowers the R code through a typed intermediate representation to generated
Fortran compiled via `R CMD SHLIB`. That IR is S7: typed values (e.g. a
`FortranSubroutine` consumed as `fsub@name`, `fsub@closure`) flow between
compiler stages. This is rung 3 of the AST escalation ladder, justified
because analysis and translation *are the product*. The broader pattern — R
syntax as source language, S7 objects as typed IR, a foreign language as
target — recurs wherever multi-target analysis appears.

### optimizers7 and parameters7 — extracting the private re-implementations

The [statmodels7](https://github.com/statmodels7) family
([optimizers7](https://github.com/statmodels7/optimizers7),
[parameters7](https://github.com/statmodels7/parameters7), with
distributions7, linkfunctions7, basis7 as siblings) is built on one sharp
observation, stated in both READMEs: almost every modeling package privately
re-implements the same mathematics — optimizers as `while (!converged)`
loops with "a tolerance compared against whatever quantity the author had to
hand," constrained parameters as bespoke parametrizations (nlme's `pdMat`,
lme4's `theta`, every mixture package's softmax) — "none exposing a
derivative, none reusable from outside."

The response is semantic atoms at the level of *mathematical behavior*: an
optimizer is an S7 object carrying its algorithm and settings, written once
against one objective interface; a **stopping rule is a separate, composable
object** — the observation that "the stopping rule, which decides what the
whole procedure means by *finished*, is usually a number buried three levels
down" is an indirection-rent argument of unusual clarity. A constrained
parameter is "a fixed mathematical object: a map from an unconstrained
vector onto the set where the parameter lives ... with its inverse, its
derivatives, and the quantities a likelihood asks of the value" —
evaluated, inverted, differentiated to fourth order, as an object. Both
packages are also deliberately *narrow* ("an optimizer here minimizes the
function it is given, with no notion of an observation") — boundary
discipline about which layer is allowed to know what.

## Cluster E — Foundations and utilities

### s7x and the R-ArcGIS stack — convergent evolution of the foundation layer

[s7x](http://s7x.josiah.rs/) (Josiah Parry) is a utility layer over S7
providing an extensible **`Enum`** class (value + variants, validated,
castable to character), **scalar properties**, **range properties**, and
**property unions and intersections**. The R-ArcGIS packages (arcgisutils,
arcgisviz) consume it at scale to model a very large TypeScript-shaped API
surface. Together with rtemis's PropertySpec factories and the private
property-factory layers appearing in document-modeling codebases, this is
now a three-way independent convergence on the same helper stratum — enum
formalization, scalar/bounded factories, presence-aware wrappers — which is
strong evidence about which foundation abstractions are genuinely
load-bearing.

### objectstore — interface-first design, embryonic

[objectstore](https://github.com/Bisaloo/objectstore) (Hugo Gruson) is an
"Object Store Interface in R with S7" at a very early stage (a handful of
commits). Its interest is the shape of the bet: defining the *abstract
interface* to object storage as the package's product, with backends to
dispatch beneath it — the generic-vocabulary-as-plugin-contract pattern
(ellmer's Providers, sqlr's dialects) applied to storage. One to watch
rather than to study yet.

### provider — the adjacent case

[provider](https://github.com/andrewallenbruce/provider) (healthcare
provider APIs) is included for completeness as a data-domain API client in
this orbit; its published surface is a tidyverse-style httr2 client rather
than an S7 architecture. It illustrates the *before* state of the patterns
in this guide — a domain of record types (providers, enrollments, claims)
currently represented as tibbles, which is entirely reasonable, and exactly
the kind of surface where semantic atoms and typed records would be the
next step if invariants started to matter.

---

## Cross-cutting observations

Reading the ecosystem as a whole rather than package by package:

**Hybrids are the norm, not the exception.** ellmer (R6 + S7), ragnar (S7 +
tibble), S7schema (S7 + list + V8/AJV), sqlr (S7 generics + S4 DBI
connections), structr (Rust boundary + plain R values), tooey (pure
functional core + runtime shell). Mature designs choose per-object semantics
and let the compatibility layer do its job.

**Constraints-as-data keeps winning.** rtemis stores property constraints in
a spec object and generates validators, schemas, and forms from it; sqlr
stores a schema as a value and generates DDL, comparisons, and diffs from
it; rapid parses OpenAPI into a strict object that generators consume;
structr compiles a schema once and parses against it. The common shape:
represent the contract as inspectable data, derive every enforcement and
projection mechanically, and never encode the same fact twice.

**Round-trip as oracle recurs independently.** sqlr's render/reflect
equality is "the package's own test oracle"; typedjson's entire product is
the identity round trip; stacbuildr writes and reads catalogs through the
same representation. When a package models a wire format, the round-trip law
is the highest-value test it can own.

**Errors have two channels, and good designs choose deliberately.**
Conditions (rlang/cli, chained, classed — datarr's `reflect_validate`) for
control-flow errors; values (resultr's `Result`, converted from conditions
at exactly one boundary) for data-flow errors. The anti-pattern is mixing
them ad hoc.

**Base-type inheritance appears exactly where it is honest.** A markdown
document is text (ragnar); an enum value is a string (s7x). Nobody publishes
a subclassed primitive stuffed with structure.

**Multiple dispatch is rare and decisive.** sqlr's `render_sql(x, con)`
(object × dialect), resultr's `expect(Success, class_character)`, S7's own
`convert(from, to)`. Everywhere it appears, the alternative was a
conditionals matrix.

**Rung 0 is always delegated.** stacbuildr to the STAC schemas, S7schema to
AJV, sqlr to the actual database engines (refusing even to pretend a generic
dialect exists), structr to a compiled Rust validator. None re-implements an
external specification internally.

**The document-object-model shape recurs across unrelated domains.**
Catalogs, configurations, conversations, styles, SQL schemas, API
descriptions, typed IRs, even terminal screens (tooey's buffer): nested
values, aggregate roots, boundary parsers, projection serializers. The
domain changes; the anatomy does not.
